candidateRows: Immediate awareness of conscious experience supplies private data that any adequate theory of reality must explain alongside public scientific data.
This establishes conscious experience as independently known evidence and supplies the epistemic foundation for Goff's case against an exclusively public-data account.
Goff distinguishes experimental observations from direct awareness of pleasures, pains, and sensory experiences, arguing that a unified theory must accommodate both categories.
Physicalism, panpsychism, and dualism are empirically equivalent interpretations of consciousness correlations, so experiments alone cannot settle the mind-body problem.
The claim determines Goff's methodology by shifting adjudication of the competing ontologies from experimental discrimination to philosophical criteria.
Using integrated information theory as an illustration, Goff argues that identical brain-consciousness correlations can be interpreted in physicalist, panpsychist, or dualist terms.
Empirically equivalent theories of mind should be compared by simplicity and by how successfully each meets its distinctive explanatory obligations.
These two criteria organize the remainder of Goff's constructive case and provide the basis for his conclusion favoring panpsychism.
Goff proposes parsimony and explanatory success, assigning physicalism the task of explaining consciousness and panpsychism the task of explaining physical reality.
Physicalism cannot explain qualitative consciousness because the quantitative vocabulary of physical science cannot articulate the qualities requiring explanation.
This is Goff's principal argument that physical explanation is structurally incapable of accounting for conscious qualities, directly supporting consciousness as fundamental.
Goff argues that neuroscience has not explained even one experience and identifies a conceptual mismatch between quantitative physical descriptions and qualitative features such as redness.
Physics succeeds at explaining publicly observable behavior, but consciousness presents a different task involving privately known and publicly inaccessible qualities.
This blocks an inference from physics's general predictive success to its ability to explain consciousness and reinforces the alleged limits of physicalist methodology.
Goff contrasts mechanism-based explanations of observable behavior with explanations of experiential qualities, comparing confidence in physics here to using telescopes for pure mathematics.
Because physics specifies only mathematical structure, networks of simple conscious entities could realize that structure and thereby ground the physical world.
This supplies Goff's positive explanation of how physical reality can arise from consciousness, completing the constructive alternative to physicalism.
Drawing on Bertrand Russell, Goff says equations constrain structure without revealing intrinsic reality, then proposes conscious entities whose interactions realize physical mathematical patterns.
Difficulty understanding an emergent phenomenon produced by billions of neurons does not justify revising an otherwise highly successful picture of physical reality.
Carroll directly contests the inference from an unresolved theory of consciousness to a fundamental revision of physics, framing his overall rebuttal to Goff.
Goff's claim that physicalism's difficulty explaining consciousness supports replacing it with a consciousness-fundamental ontology.
Carroll grants that consciousness is difficult and that alternatives are possible, but uses a mathematical-homework analogy to argue against challenging secure foundations first.
Weak emergence permits consciousness to be a valid higher-level description of the same physical reality described microscopically by quantum fields and biologically by neurons.
This is Carroll's principal positive physicalist model, explaining how conscious vocabulary can be real and useful without adding fundamental nonphysical entities.
Goff's contention that qualitative consciousness cannot intelligibly emerge from quantitative physical processes.

After noting interaction problems for nonphysical minds, Carroll develops layered vocabularies through thermodynamics, neuroscience, and human agency, stressing compatibility across descriptive levels.
Although consciousness is not yet understood, mapping physical brain processes, mental events, and their relations constitutes an active and promising physicalist research program.
The move answers the alleged explanatory stagnation of physicalism by identifying a concrete empirical program and presenting observed brain-thought correlations as progress.
Goff's assertion that physicalism has made no explanatory progress on even a single conscious experience.

Carroll concedes ignorance about the finished explanation, then describes correlating mental activity with brain and body processes, including magnetoencephalographic measurements of his own thoughts.
Mary's new experience of red is compatible with physicalism because seeing red produces a different physical brain state from merely reading all available descriptions of red.
This rebuts a canonical argument that experiential knowledge exceeds physical facts and directly defends physicalism against an influential qualitative-consciousness objection.
The knowledge argument that learning what red looks like after knowing every physical fact establishes nonphysical qualia.
Carroll recounts Mary's confinement and apparent new knowledge, questions the clarity of knowing every physical fact, and explains the experiential change through differing neural activation.
Established particle physics tightly constrains every interaction relevant to biology, thought, and consciousness despite gaps elsewhere in science.
This establishes the empirical foundation for Carroll's argument that consciousness requires no presently unknown particles, forces, or biological physics.
After completing his answer to the knowledge argument, Carroll carefully distinguishes incomplete science from the well-tested core theory governing human-scale physical interactions.
Any specific panpsychist theory must say whether it changes the core physical theory, and either answer carries substantial argumentative burdens.
The dilemma directly structures Carroll's central objection to consciousness-first theories and demands a concrete account of their relation to tested physics.
Goff's panpsychist proposal that consciousness underlies the physical structures described by science.
Building on the core theory's empirical success, Carroll argues that a physics-changing panpsychism must specify new dynamics and reconcile them with existing evidence.
A panpsychism that leaves physical dynamics unchanged adds nothing to physical explanation and risks making consciousness causally irrelevant to behavior.
This supplies the other horn of Carroll's core dilemma by arguing that empirically inert consciousness cannot explain the behavioral phenomenon at issue.
The proposal that panpsychism can preserve ordinary physical dynamics while adding consciousness as their underlying reality.
Carroll turns from physics-modifying theories to theories that preserve the core theory, using philosophical zombies to connect explanatory relevance with behavioral effects.
A physical explanation of experiential qualities would make their qualitative character fully intelligible in quantitative neuroscientific terms, which it cannot do.
This restates Goff's principal case against physicalism by locating the explanatory gap between quantitative neural descriptions and qualitative experience.
Carroll's claim that differing neural activity fully accounts for the Mary thought experiment without challenging physicalism.
Goff says Carroll has mistaken the knowledge argument for a question about producing an experience, then reframes it as a question about grasping qualitative character.
Physicalists must either abandon an intelligible explanation of consciousness or accept that neuroscience alone could convey what seeing red is like.
The dilemma converts Goff's explanatory-gap argument into a direct burden for physicalism and explains why he regards reduction as conceptually unavailable.
Carroll's expectation that consciousness can eventually be explained while retaining the established physicalist framework.
Goff contrasts scientific physicalists who seek an explanation with philosophical physicalists who doubt one is possible, arguing their combined commitments undermine physicalism.
The possibility of a physically identical zombie world does not make consciousness causally idle because the same physical structure can have different realizers.
This directly defends panpsychism against Carroll's behavioral irrelevance objection by separating a realized structure from the nature of its realizing basis.
Carroll's argument that conceivable behavioral duplicates without consciousness render consciousness causally and evidentially irrelevant.
Goff compares physics to software and consciousness to hardware, arguing that possible realization in nonconscious material does not show conscious realizers do nothing.
Panpsychism need not conflict with current physics because weak-emergent versions preserve physical equations while positing a deeper conscious basis beneath them.
This answers Carroll's principal dilemma by identifying a coherent panpsychist option that retains tested physical predictions while adding an underlying ontology.
Carroll's dilemma requiring panpsychism either to alter the tested core theory or become explanatorily dispensable.
Goff calls the claimed clash a red herring, notes that strong and weak emergent versions exist on both sides, and locates consciousness beneath unchanged physics.
Conscious awareness is an independent datum that theories of reality must integrate with experimental science even when experiments cannot distinguish their metaphysical claims.
The passage explains why empirically equivalent panpsychism remains philosophically significant and supplies Goff's criterion for comparing competing accounts of reality.
Carroll's claim that a theory leaving physical understanding unchanged gives him no substantive reason to care about it.
Goff rejects an exclusively experimental standard, arguing that immediate awareness of consciousness must be reconciled with scientific knowledge through explanatory comparison.
Science's experimental success does not establish physicalism, while panpsychism can jointly explain quantitative physical structure and qualitative consciousness.
This is Goff's culminating comparative case: empirical equivalence leaves a philosophical choice that he says favors panpsychism's broader explanatory reach.
Carroll's reliance on the success of physical science as the strongest basis for treating the physical world as fundamental.
Goff argues that natural science succeeds through a deliberately narrow experimental focus, whereas a complete worldview must also accommodate directly known qualitative experience.
The success of the physical picture makes it the best provisional basis for future progress, and panpsychism must still answer whether it changes known physics.
This rebuts the scientism charge and reasserts Carroll's principal comparative reason and unresolved dilemma against Goff's panpsychist position.
Goff's claim that Carroll merely assumes physicalism because it appears scientific and that weak panpsychism answers the core-theory objection.
Carroll denies treating physicalism as dogma, presents it as a fallible evidential bet, and argues that Goff has not clearly chosen between altering and preserving physics.
Positing consciousness as fundamental does not explain conscious experience unless it clarifies why particular experiences occur and affect behavior.
This establishes Carroll's principal objection that fundamental consciousness supplies no explanatory path from ontology to particular experiences, circumstances, and behavior.
Goff's claim that panpsychism explains conscious experience by treating consciousness as fundamental.
Carroll distinguishes a merely fundamental posit from an explanation of persons, experiences, and behavior, arguing that panpsychism leaves the relevant connections unspecified.
Science may use private as well as public data and seeks the empirically best account compatible with the full body of available evidence.
The move contests the methodological premise that modern science is restricted to quantitative or publicly observable data, which supports Goff's case against physicalism.
Goff's contention that post-Galilean science is confined to quantitative descriptions and excludes qualitative consciousness.
Carroll broadens science to include all available data, including thought and private experience, while retaining empirical comparison among candidate explanations.
A complete multilevel mapping among physical states, conscious experience, behavior, and dynamics would count as an explanation of consciousness.
It gives the physicalist side's affirmative explanatory standard and identifies the central disagreement over whether perfect structural and dynamical understanding is sufficient.
Goff's claim that physical accounts leave the subjective qualitative character of consciousness unexplained in principle.
Carroll argues that science legitimately posits unobservables for explanatory purposes and can connect quarks, neurons, agents, experience, and behavior through compatible levels of description.
The hard problem will dissolve as increasingly precise neuroscience connects reported conscious experiences with brain states and behavior.
This is a direct physicalist answer to the debate's central explanatory challenge, predicting dissolution rather than a separate fundamental solution to subjective experience.
Goff's position that subjective experience creates an in-principle explanatory barrier for physicalism.
Carroll maintains that improved correlations among experience, brain activity, perception, and action will remove the motivation for treating the hard problem as an additional ontological problem.
Mary's acquisition of new knowledge about what seeing red is like shows that a complete neuroscientific account omits information about experience.
The argument directly supports the fundamental-consciousness side by claiming that even complete physical information cannot exhaust the essential nature of conscious experience.
Carroll's claim that the knowledge argument merely confuses learning physical facts with undergoing the corresponding sensory experience.
Goff distinguishes gaining an experience from gaining information, arguing that Mary learns a new fact after seeing red and therefore lacked a complete account beforehand.
Panpsychism explains physical reality in terms of consciousness and thereby offers a unified account grounded in one fundamental kind of reality.
This supplies the positive explanatory case for the pro side: consciousness is not merely labeled fundamental, but is proposed as the basis from which physical structure is derived.
Carroll's repeated objection that declaring consciousness fundamental explains nothing and offers only an intuitive sense of satisfaction.
Goff says Russellian construction can account for physical structure through underlying conscious facts, allowing both consciousness and physics to be unified in a consciousness-first ontology.
Because consciousness is privately known rather than publicly observed, an adequate theory must integrate it with physical reality instead of limiting explanation to experimental observables.
The move defends consciousness as genuine explanatory data and explains why complete neuroscience would still leave an ontological integration question unanswered.
Carroll's argument that science can include unobservable entities whenever they contribute to an empirically successful explanatory theory.
Goff distinguishes postulating unseen entities to explain public observations from explaining consciousness itself, which is privately known and must be reconciled with the physical world.
Whether panpsychism changes established physics is not a relevant contrast with physicalism because versions of either view may preserve or reject the core theory.
This neutralizes Carroll's proposed decision point by arguing that compatibility with established physics cross-cuts the panpsychism-versus-physicalism distinction.
Carroll's demand that Goff specify whether his panpsychism changes the empirically established core theory of physics.
Goff rejects a single yes-or-no answer for panpsychism as a category, observing that both panpsychist and physicalist theories can be formulated compatibly or incompatibly with current physics.
Treating consciousness as an additional fundamental feature adds no explanation unless it changes physics and generates assessable empirical consequences.
The move crystallizes Carroll's criterion for theoretical gain and directly challenges nonphysical ontology that preserves every physical prediction while adding no empirical structure.
Goff's claim that a consciousness-first ontology unifies private experience and physical reality even without changing established physics.
Using the dispute over whether laws are separate governing entities, Carroll argues that an added metaphysical posit explains nothing unless it changes the theory in testable and consequential ways.
A physically and behaviorally identical duplicate would be equally conscious because consciousness is a higher-level concept instantiated by the underlying physical organization.
The response rejects philosophical zombies and affirms the physicalist identity between appropriate physical organization and consciousness, directly bearing on causal efficacy and emergence.
The audience challenge suggesting that consciousness can be removed while the physical world or physical functioning remains unchanged.

Carroll says consciousness affects behavior, denies that atom-for-atom behavioral duplicates could lack experience, and treats consciousness as a human-level description compatible with physical processes.
Neither physicalism nor pansychism can provide more than relational and behavioral answers about the intrinsic character of seeing red.
The move directly contests the claim that an unexplained qualitative remainder uniquely exposes a deficiency in physicalist accounts of experience.
The audience member's claim that complete neurological information still leaves Fred's distinctive color experience unexplained.

An audience member uses Fred's enhanced color vision to argue that neuroscience leaves subjective appearance unspecified; Sean disputes that any rival theory supplies the requested intrinsic description.
The difficulty of answering the knowledge argument cannot be dismissed as a mere demand for satisfaction, as shown by sustained physicalist efforts to answer it.
The move defends a central anti-physicalist argument by denying that Sean's relational account resolves the underlying explanatory challenge.
Sean's contention that only relational descriptions of color experience are available under any metaphysical theory.
After Sean says no theory can offer more than relational answers about seeing red, Philip argues that this response understates the established difficulty of the knowledge argument.
If a behaviorally identical zombie is conceivable, nonphysical consciousness is thereby conceived as making no difference to behavior.
This is a direct causal-exclusion objection: conceivability of an exact behavioral duplicate threatens any claimed explanatory role for nonphysical consciousness.
The questioner's attempt to understand how consciousness, thought, behavior, and philosophical zombies can be correlated.
Sean clarifies that philosophical zombies must duplicate all human behavior, then argues that accepting their conceivability removes nonphysical consciousness from the behavioral explanation.
Identical behavior can be multiply realized, so a conscious person's behavior may be grounded in consciousness while a zombie's is grounded nonconsciously.
The move directly blocks Sean's causal-exclusion inference and restates the claimed distinction between behavioral facts and facts about felt experience.
Sean's argument that conceivability of an exact behavioral zombie makes nonphysical consciousness behaviorally causally idle.
Philip answers the zombie objection by invoking multiple realization and maintains that claims about pain concern how someone feels, not merely external or internal behavior.
The combination problem remains pansychism's major challenge, but it is comparatively young, not demonstrably insoluble, and separable from the theory's monistic appeal.
The move concedes and contains the principal objection to pansychism while preserving its claimed advantage of explaining physical reality through one fundamental kind.
The standing objection that small conscious entities cannot intelligibly combine into unified human-scale consciousness.

Philip acknowledges the combination problem, cites active research, contrasts its short history with physicalism's hard problem, and argues that pansychism's core monism survives even without reduction.
Quantum interpretations are genuinely different physical theories, so they provide no precedent for redescribing one unchanged core theory as fundamentally conscious.
The move rejects a proposed route for adding fundamental consciousness without physical differences and reconnects that rejection to the zombie and device analogies.
The questioner's proposal that the same physical core theory could admit both conscious and nonconscious fundamental interpretations.
Asked whether quantum-mechanical interpretive plurality licenses a conscious interpretation of the core theory, Sean argues that the quantum cases actually differ physically rather than verbally.
Private experience is compatible with physicalism, and consciousness's exceptional difficulty is expected rather than evidence that physical explanation must fail.
The move directly addresses whether first-person conscious data undermine physicalism and supplies an epistemic reason for expecting present explanatory incompleteness.
The questioner's suggestion that rich inner life and extraordinary experiences may resist or exceed a physicalist understanding.

Sean says his inner data fit his physical worldview, treats current ignorance as unsurprising given consciousness's difficulty, and sees no experiential reason to expect permanent physical inexplicability.
First-person data could support physicalism only if it intelligibly derived qualitative experience from quantitative processes, an obligation physicalism has not fulfilled.
The move states the decisive condition under which physicalism could succeed and argues that conceptual disparity and historical failure count against its fulfillment.
The audience question asking whether properly valued first-person private data could ever lead an investigator toward physicalism.
Philip grants physicalism a possible path in principle but says it would require an intelligible emergence account comparable to ordinary scientific reductions, which he argues has been abandoned.
Science broadly includes private qualitative evidence as empirical data and remains the appropriate method for understanding what the world is and how it works.
The move denies that physical inquiry excludes consciousness merely because experience is private, thereby defending science's methodological reach over the debate's subject.
The questioner's concern that looking only through physical science may impose limits or leave important aspects of reality unexplained.

Sean defines science as empirical hypothesis testing broad enough to include inner experience, while separating descriptive understanding of reality from subjective preferences and constructed values.
A theory of reality must synthesize experimental findings with consciousness and other non-scientific data, and pansychism offers a unified framework for doing so.
The move closes the debate with a methodological case for treating consciousness as irreducible evidence and for preferring a unified consciousness-based metaphysics.
Sean's position that broadly empirical science includes private experience and is sufficient for understanding how reality works.
Philip agrees that experiments and observation matter but adds consciousness, value, mathematics, and logic, presenting philosophy as their synthesis into a simple unified account.
